content: Vibrio is a genus of Gram-negative bacteria characterized by a curved rod shape. These bacteria are commonly found in saltwater environments and are facultative anaerobes, meaning they can survive in both oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor conditions. They test positive for oxidase activity and do not form spores. All members of the Vibrio genus are motile and possess polar flagella that are covered by a sheath. Recent phylogenetic studies have been conducted using multi-locus sequence analysis, which involves examining a suite of genes to better understand their evolutionary relationships. Several species of Vibrio are clinically significant human pathogens. Most disease-causing strains are associated with gastroenteritis, but they can also infect open wounds and lead to septicemia. Vibrio can be carried by various marine animals, such as crabs and prawns, and exposure to these bacteria has been known to cause fatal infections in humans. Notable pathogenic species include Vibrio cholerae (the causative agent of cholera), Vibrio parahaemolyticus, and Vibrio vulnificus. Vibrio cholerae is typically transmitted through contaminated water. Pathogenic Vibrio species are also known to cause foodborne illnesses, often linked to the consumption of undercooked seafood. Outbreaks of Vibrio vulnificus are more common in warm climates and frequently result in small but highly lethal outbreaks. For example, an outbreak occurred in New Orleans following Hurricane Katrina, and several fatal cases are reported annually in Florida. Vibrio parahaemolyticus is associated with the Kanagawa phenomenon, where strains isolated from human hosts (clinical isolates) exhibit hemolytic activity on blood agar plates, while those isolated from non-human sources are non-hemolytic. Many Vibrio species are also zoonotic, causing diseases in fish and shellfish. They are a common cause of mortality in domesticated marine life. Other Vibrio species, such as Vibrio fischeri, Photobacterium phosphoreum, and Vibrio harveyi, are notable for their ability to communicate through quorum sensing. Both Vibrio fischeri and Photobacterium phosphoreum are symbionts of marine organisms, such as jellyfish, fish, and squid, and they produce light via bioluminescence. Vibrio harveyi is a pathogen of several aquatic animals and is known to cause luminous vibriosis in shrimp. The flagellar structure of Vibrio species varies. The typical Vibrio species, such as Vibrio cholerae, have a single polar flagellum (monotrichous) with a sheath. Some species, such as Vibrio parahaemolyticus and Vibrio alginolyticus, possess both a single polar flagellum with a sheath and thin flagella projecting in all directions (peritrichous). Other species, such as Vibrio fischeri, have tufts of polar flagella with a sheath (lophotrichous).
